analysis.one_liner: Ordered OSHA to issue emergency COVID-19 worker-safety rules for health care and other high-risk jobs.
analysis.headline: Introduced March 25, 2020, the bill was referred to the Senate HELP Committee and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Labor Department to quickly issue emergency workplace safety rules protecting health care workers, paramedics, and other high-risk workers from COVID-19 exposure, including an infectious disease exposure control plan. It would have made those rules permanent within two years, directed the CDC to track COVID-19 cases among covered workers, and required hospitals and nursing homes not otherwise covered by safety law to follow the standard as a condition of Medicare funding.
analysis.who_benefits: Health care workers, first responders, and other workers at elevated risk of COVID-19 exposure, who would gain enforceable protections like exposure control plans and personal protective equipment requirements.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Health care and other high-risk workers

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Labor Department to issue an emergency temporary standard within one month protecting health care, paramedic, and other elevated-risk workers from workplace COVID-19 exposure [S2][S3].
Requires a permanent infectious-pathogen standard within 24 months, and ties Medicare funding for hospitals and nursing homes not covered by OSHA to compliance [S2][S3].
Directs the CDC to collect data on and investigate work-related COVID-19 cases among covered workers and report publicly [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health care employers — hospitals, nursing homes, EMS providers — and other covered employers, who would bear the cost of exposure control plans, protective equipment, and compliance.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs could strain hospitals and nursing homes already stretched thin during the pandemic, and the bill includes enforcement discretion for employers that cannot immediately obtain protective equipment, acknowledging feasibility limits [S3].
A federal requirement reaching state and local government employers (like public hospitals and EMS) raises federalism concerns, since OSHA historically excludes state and local governments [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For frontline workers facing the highest exposure risk in the deadliest months of the pandemic, enforceable federal safety rules offered real protection at a modest compliance cost to employers, some of it offset by reduced worker illness.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate HELP Committee, which never acted on it before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Introduced March 25, 2020 by Senator Baldwin with one cosponsor (Senator Duckworth) and read twice, then referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee [S1][S3][S5].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and died when the 116th Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health care employers — hospitals, nursing homes, and EMS providers — avoided new mandatory exposure-control standards, protective equipment requirements, and Medicare funding conditions during the pandemic.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health care employers avoiding new mandates

for.name: Tammy Baldwin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring emergency COVID-19 workplace safety standards.

for.name: Tammy Duckworth
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as one of its two original sponsors.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup on the referred bill, letting it die without action.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no position can be inferred beyond its two Democratic sponsors; the record shows no action by others.

industries.note: The bill would have required these facilities to implement exposure control plans and protective equipment, and tied Medicare funding to compliance for facilities not covered by OSHA. The cost of compliance falls on them, while the benefit of safer workplaces goes to workers.
Paramedic and EMS employers, including fire-based services, would have been subject to the emergency standard's requirements.
